title: Spain and Argentina Set for World Cup Final as Messi's Last Dance Meets Falklands Controversy
excerpt: Sunday's final at MetLife Stadium pits the defending champions against the Euro 2024 winners, with the buildup dominated by a diplomatic row over an Argentine banner and the question of whether Messi's career ends in triumph or defeat.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Spain faces Argentina in the World Cup final at MetLife Stadium, kicking off at 4 PM ET.
  • Lionel Messi, at 39, may be playing his last World Cup match.
  • Spain has scored 16 goals in six matches, while Argentina has conceded four.
  • Argentina's semifinal win sparked a diplomatic row over a political banner about the Falklands.
  • The final is expected to attract over 1.5 billion viewers worldwide.
  • Spain face defending champions Argentina in Sunday's World Cup final at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, kicking off at 4 PM ET.
  • At 39, Messi is playing what is almost certainly his last World Cup. If Spain win, 19-year-old Lamine Yamal would become the youngest World Cup winner since 1982.
  • Argentina rallied from behind to beat England 2-1 in the semifinals, but the aftermath was overshadowed by players displaying a political banner about the Falkland Islands.
  • FIFA is facing pressure from British officials to sanction Argentine players, though disqualification from the final is considered unlikely.

The 2026 FIFA World Cup final is set. Spain will face defending champions Argentina on Sunday at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, in a match that brings together two of football's most compelling narratives — the probable end of Lionel Messi's international career and the potential coronation of his 19-year-old Barcelona successor, Lamine Yamal.

Messi's Last Stand

Argentina came within six minutes of elimination in their semifinal against England on Wednesday before rallying to win 2-1. It was the latest in a series of narrow escapes for the defending champions, who survived scares against Cape Verde, Egypt, and Switzerland earlier in the tournament.

For Messi, now 39, the story of this World Cup has been one of diminishing minutes but undimmed influence. His through-ball in the 84th minute against England set up the equalizer, and his leadership in Argentina's counterattacks showed the tactical intelligence that compensates for legs that no longer carry him past defenders at full speed.

The question is whether that can be enough against a Spanish side that has dominated the tournament. Spain have scored 16 goals in six matches and conceded just three, combining the pressing intensity of their Euro 2024 triumph with a squad that is deeper and more physically mature than the one that won in Berlin last summer.

Yamal's Coronation

If Spain win on Sunday, Yamal would become the youngest player to lift the World Cup since Giuseppe Bergomi with Italy in 1982. He would also be the first player in history to win both the European Championship and the World Cup before turning 20.

At Barcelona, Yamal has already inherited Messi's number 10 shirt and much of his creative burden. On Sunday, the two will share a pitch for perhaps the last time — the heir against the legend in a contest that carries symbolic weight for Spanish and Argentine football alike.

The Falklands Shadow

The buildup has been consumed by a diplomatic row that has nothing to do with tactics. After Argentina's semifinal win, several players held up a white banner reading "Las Malvinas Son Argentinas" — The Falklands Are Argentine — during on-pitch celebrations.

A Reuters photograph showed the homemade banner initially waved by fans in the front rows before midfielder Giovani Lo Celso approached and asked to borrow it, holding it up alongside centre-back Lisandro Martínez.

British business minister Peter Kyle told BBC Radio the incident must be formally investigated. Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey wrote to FIFA President Gianni Infantino demanding the offending players be disqualified from the final.

FIFA's Stadium Code of Conduct bans political banners and paraphernalia. Precedent suggests a fine rather than a sporting ban: Argentina paid roughly £20,000 for an almost identical Falklands display at the 2014 World Cup. Spain's Rodri and Álvaro Morata received one-match international bans after chanting "Gibraltar is Spain" during Euro 2024 celebrations, but those sanctions were applied after the tournament concluded.

In Buenos Aires, the public backed the players. "The Malvinas are ours, everyone knows it," a local told Reuters, reflecting the depth of feeling that has shaped Argentine politics since the 1982 conflict that claimed 904 lives.

A Tactical Clash of Styles

On the pitch, the final presents a genuine tactical puzzle. Spain's high-possession, high-press system thrives against teams that try to hold the ball, but Argentina under Lionel Scaloni have proven throughout the tournament that they can absorb pressure and strike on the counter with devastating efficiency.

Argentina's defense, organized around Cristian Romero and Martínez, has conceded just four goals in the tournament. But they have not faced an attack as varied as Spain's, which can score through Yamal's dribbling, Pedri's passing, and Álvaro Morata's aerial presence.

Bookmakers have Spain as slight favorites, reflecting their dominant run through the tournament. But Argentina's experience in knockout football — this is their third final in four World Cups — makes them dangerous underdogs.

A Global Audience

The match kicks off at 4 PM ET on Sunday, with a worldwide audience expected to exceed 1.5 billion. Across the Indian diaspora, the final has captured public attention like few sporting events outside cricket. Delhi authorities have granted cafes permission to stay open until 4 AM, while viewing parties have been organized in Indian communities from Hyderabad to Houston.

Whether Sunday is remembered as Messi's farewell triumph or Yamal's breakthrough moment, it promises to be a fitting conclusion to a tournament that has delivered more drama than any since 2014.
